title: ⭐⭐ Practice: why you did it, and whether you still do

questions.prompt: A pupil writes about her grandfather: "Every summer he would take us to the sea, and we would stay until September." What does would express here?

options.text: A condition that was never met.
A polite request made to the family.
A habit repeated over a closed period.
Something the grandfather still intends to do this year.

questions.explanation: Every summer sets a stretch of past time and the two verbs describe what happened again and again inside it, which is the past-habit use of would. A condition would need an if somewhere in the sentence, and there is none — that is the single test that separates this would from the conditional one. A request would be addressed to somebody, in a question such as would you take us, and here the grandfather is spoken about rather than spoken to. And an intention would point forward, which every summer and the past tense of stay together rule out.

questions.prompt: Complete with the right structure: "She is taking evening classes ……… better qualifications."

options.text: in order to have
so that have
for to have
so that to have obtained

questions.explanation: The same person takes the classes and gets the qualifications, so a structure followed by a plain verb is what the sentence needs, and in order to have is exactly the example your book prints in its grammar box. so that would be possible only with a subject after it, as in so that she can have better qualifications; written without one it is simply incomplete. Putting for in front of to is a mistake English never makes, however natural it feels in French. And combining so that with to piles the two structures on top of each other, keeping the weakness of both.

questions.prompt: Thorson explains why he came to Japan and what he hopes to do afterwards. Which of these does the recording actually say about his childhood?

options.text: He wanted to be a fireman.
He wanted to be a diplomat even then.
He wanted to be a baseball player.
He had no dream at all and still has none.

questions.explanation: He says that as a child he wanted to be a baseball player, so that he could be famous the world over — and the purpose clause is why the lesson keeps the detail. The fireman is in the recording too, but as something he explicitly denies: he says he never went through that stage. Diplomat is his ambition now, and the question asks about his childhood, which is the only thing separating the two answers. And he is far from having no dream: he ends the interview by saying he is still dreaming, which is what makes the exchange worth listening to.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the odd one out, because its verb is not a past habit?

options.text: Camel trains used to carry all the goods between Africa and Europe.
Each animal often carried as much as four hundred pounds.
Traders would put together camel trains of fifteen thousand animals.
This form of transport used to be the only one available.

questions.explanation: The sentence about four hundred pounds is an ordinary past simple, and the word often is already doing the work of repetition, which is exactly why your book does not use a habit form there. The other three all announce a habit explicitly: two with used to, which adds the meaning that it is no longer so, and one with would, which repeats an action across a closed stretch of time. This is the point the camel exercise is built to make — a past that repeats does not always need a special form, and piling one on when the adverb already says it is the commonest way to overwork the structure.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 20, Patricia dropped her son at the childminder's house at seven in the morning, and the childminder picked him up again after school. What do the two verbs describe?

options.text: Letting something fall to the ground, and then lifting it again.
Leaving somebody somewhere, and collecting them.
Abandoning a child, and adopting one.
Refusing a job, and accepting another.

questions.explanation: to drop somebody means to leave them somewhere on your way to another place, and to pick somebody up means to go and collect them; together they mark the two ends of the same working day, which is why the lesson uses them side by side. Letting something fall is the everyday meaning of drop applied to an object, and it has nothing to do with a person you leave at an address. Abandoning and adopting are far stronger than what happened, and the text is careful to say the boy was fond of the childminder. And nothing in either verb concerns accepting or refusing work.

questions.prompt: A careers leaflet says: "An internship is a period of practical training inside a workplace." Which of these people is doing an internship, as Heidrun describes hers?

options.text: A student spending two years in a hospital as part of her course.
A doctor who has finished her studies and now runs her own private clinic.
A pupil visiting a hospital for one afternoon with her class.
A patient going into hospital for a check-up.

questions.explanation: Heidrun says that of her four to six years of college, two are spent in a hospital as an intern, which matches the leaflet exactly: training that is practical, that happens inside a workplace, and that belongs to a course of study. A doctor running her own clinic has finished training altogether — that is the stage Heidrun hopes to reach afterwards. A single afternoon with a class is a visit, not a period of training, and nothing about it forms part of a qualification. And a patient having a check-up is being treated rather than trained, which is the other side of the same room.
